findings.paper_title: TDC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: Grounds maintenance contract not mobilised fully and changes to scope manual and incomplete
findings.detail: The contractor has not mobilised all services as defined in the contract. Identification of changes required to the contract schedule is being done manually, is time-consuming, and is not yet complete, delaying understanding of whether changes may affect budget provision. Contract management meetings were not in line with contract-specified frequency.
findings.matters: Incomplete contract mobilisation and unclear impact of scope changes on budget create cost control risk; manual, incomplete change management suggests budgetary slippage.
findings.figures: Contract management meetings not in line with specified frequency; scope change process not yet complete
findings.quote: Additionally, the contractor had not mobilised all services and processes as defined within the contract. We also found that the identification of changes required by the Council to the contract schedule in terms of what facilities/locations required to be covered is having to be done manually and is time consuming and not yet complete, delaying the understanding of whether changes may have a significant impact on budget provision.

findings.paper_title: TDC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: Social housing regulator issued a C4 (Consumer) rating in September 2025, requiring fundamental changes
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing concluded that the council has 'very serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards' and that 'the landlord must make fundamental changes so that improved outcomes are delivered.' The council is continuing to work with the regulator.
findings.matters: A C4 housing regulator rating signals severe operational and governance failures in a major council service; this indicates both reputational and delivery risk, and may affect the council's standing with government.
findings.figures: C4 rating (Consumer standard) issued September 2025
findings.quote: The Regulators report and judgement was issued in September 2025, concluding a C4 rating (Consumer) - Our judgement is that there are very serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards. The landlord must make fundamental changes so that improved outcomes are delivered.

findings.paper_title: TDC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: Business continuity plans missing for half of essential services, with no testing of those in place
findings.detail: The council identified 16 services as essential and required to have business continuity plans. Only 8 had been developed, none had been tested, 3 lacked service manager approval, and 2 had no stakeholder planning. The audit gave this area a No Assurance opinion — the lowest rating.
findings.matters: A council unable to execute business continuity for half its essential services poses operational and service delivery risk; lenders need confidence in operational resilience.
findings.figures: 8 of 16 essential services with a BCP in place; zero testing completed on those 8
findings.quote: however, we identified that of 16 BCP's that should be in place only 8 had been developed. Furthermore, for the 8 BCPs in place no testing of plans had been undertaken, 3 had yet to be approved by service managers and 2 had nothing listed within the internal/external stakeholder section of the plan.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Update
findings.headline: Asset revaluation accounting policy change will reduce council costs and valuation complexity from April 2025.
findings.detail: CIPFA Code now allows a 5-year valuation cycle for operational property, plant and equipment with indexation in between years, replacing frequent full revaluations. Tandridge has adopted this approach, which will "significantly reduce costs" and "simplify asset valuation requirements."
findings.matters: Cost reduction and simpler accounting improve financial management efficiency and reduce distraction from audit challenges, though it also means assets are revalued less frequently.
findings.figures: 5-year revaluation cycle from 1 April 2025
findings.quote: This change follows HM Treasury's Thematic Review on Non-investment Assets and is intended to reduce valuation costs, complexity and audit challenges.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Update
findings.headline: Auditors have developed a "Regaining Assurance Strategy" for Tandridge, indicating need to rebuild audit confidence.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's strategy document (Appendix B) suggests systematic work is needed to restore audit assurance. The title itself signals prior audit challenges that require structured recovery.
findings.matters: A bespoke recovery strategy indicates the auditors have lost confidence in the council's audit trail or controls and must work to rebuild it.
findings.figures: Strategy period: July 2026 onwards
findings.quote: Note the External Auditors "Regaining Assurance Strategy for Tandridge District Council", as set-out in Appendix B.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Update
findings.headline: Council finance team is stretched, with loss of Surrey County Council support and Local Government Reorganisation adding pressure.
findings.detail: As of April 2025, Tandridge lost external audit cover from Surrey County Council and must deliver audit-readiness internally. Combined with LGR pressures while maintaining business as usual, the finance team is described as "already stretched." The council met the 30 June 2026 draft accounts deadline despite this, but the report notes this is a "fantastic achievement" precisely because resources are limited.
findings.matters: A stretched finance team increases risk of error, delayed reporting, or reduced financial control quality. It also makes the council vulnerable to further audit problems.
findings.figures: Draft accounts deadline: 30 June 2026 (met); audit support lost April 2025
findings.quote: With the additional pressure that Local Government Reorganisation brings to the Council on top of ensuring businesses as usual continues as before has brought additional demands to an already stretched team.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Update
findings.headline: Audit fee dispute of £410k for 2019–2022 is being actively challenged with legal counsel.
findings.detail: Auditors originally claimed £658k against contracted fees of £107k. PSAA reduced this to £517k, leaving £410k variation. The council disputes this and has commissioned barristers to assist. The 2021/22 fees alone are noted as "greatly larger than the original contract value." This remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Unresolved fee disputes indicate audit relationship stress and potential future cost exposure; £410k is material to a district council.
findings.figures: Original contracted fees 2019–2022: £107k; auditors claimed: £658k; PSAA agreed: £517k; amount owed: £410k
findings.quote: The original annual contracted fees for the 3 years between 2019-2022 was £35,536 and a total of £107k. £658k was the total costs claimed by the auditors for same period. PSSA carried out in depth audits on the fees claimed. This concluded in a reduction for the 3 years of £141k from the original claim taking the total fees to £517k. This gave an overall fee variation for years 2019-2022 of £410k.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Update
findings.headline: Grant Thornton expects to issue a disclaimed audit opinion for 2025/26 due to lack of assurance over prior-year balances.
findings.detail: The auditors cannot provide assurance over brought-forward balances that were deprioritised in the 2023/24 audit. This means they have no assurance over all in-year movements or comparative prior-year movements. A disclaimed opinion is material and indicates significant audit gaps for the financial year being audited.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on audited accounts; a disclaimed opinion means no independent verification of the council's financial position for 2025/26.
findings.figures: 2025/26 audit scheduled mid-September to November 2026
findings.quote: The reason for the auditor's opinion being disclaimed is due to the auditor's do not have assurance over brought forward balances that were deprioritised on the 2023/24 audit. This means they do not have assurance over all in-year movements. Nor do the auditors have assurance over the comparative prior year movements.

findings.paper_title: 202526 Budget Outturn - Housing Committee_v3
findings.headline: £527k Housing Improvement Plan funded ahead of Social Housing Regulator review
findings.detail: The council approved £420k in September 2025 and an additional £107k in November 2025 from HRA reserves to fund a Housing Improvement Plan in advance of a Social Housing Regulator review. The timing and scale of spending suggests material compliance or performance issues requiring remedial action.
findings.matters: Social Housing Regulator reviews can identify compliance gaps and require remedial action. Voluntary improvement spending of this magnitude signals management acknowledgement of deficiencies that the regulator has flagged.
findings.figures: £420k approved September 2025; £107k approved November 2025; total £527k
findings.quote: Since the setting of the budget, £420k was moved from the HRA net operating surplus to fund an initial Housing Improvement Plan (HIP) in advance of the review by the Social Housing Regulator. This was approved at Strategy and Resources Committee on 25th September 2025. In addition £107k was agreed to be added to the Housing Improvement Plan and approved at Housing Committee on 13th November 2025.

findings.paper_title: 202526 Budget Outturn - Housing Committee_v3
findings.headline: HRA borrowing increased £9.1m year-on-year to £76.5m, a 13.5% increase
findings.detail: Total HRA borrowing rose from £67.4m at 1 April 2025 to £76.5m at 31 March 2026, comprising internal borrowing of £25.8m and external PWLB borrowing of £50.7m. The £9.1m increase represents significant growth in the council's debt burden in a single year.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in debt levels is a key credit risk indicator for lenders. The 13.5% year-on-year increase, particularly given simultaneous capital delivery failures, raises questions about financial sustainability and debt serviceability.
findings.figures: Opening borrowing £67.4m (£18m internal, £49.4m external); Closing borrowing £76.5m (£25.8m internal, £50.7m external); increase £9.1m
findings.quote: The borrowings as at 1st April 2025 were £67.4m which was financed through a combination of internal and external borrowing (PWLB) of £18m and £49.4m respectively. The position at year end are total borrowings of £76.5m of which £25.8m is internal borrowing and £50.7m is external borrowing (PWLB).

findings.paper_title: 202526 Budget Outturn - Housing Committee_v3
findings.headline: HRA Capital Programme rephased mid-year by £6.2m, then underspent by £5.8m—£12m total capital reduction against initial plan
findings.detail: The HRA Capital Programme began at £26.6m and was increased to £30.4m with carry-forwards. In September, it was rephased down to £24.1m (£6.2m reduction). Final outturn was £18.3m, creating a £5.8m underspend against the rephased budget. Combined, the council failed to deliver £12m (40%) of planned capital investment.
findings.matters: Multiple levels of forecast failure indicate weak project planning and delivery capability. An inability to accurately forecast capital spend twice (at rephase and outturn) raises questions about management control and project viability.
findings.figures: Original budget £26,566k + carry-forwards £3,804k = £30,370k; rephased to £24,148k; outturn £18,311k
findings.quote: For the Housing Revenue Account, a budget including carry-forwards and adjustments of £24,148k was available, as set out in paragraphs 5-6. The final outturn is £18,311k, with a net variance of (£5,837k) against budget.

findings.paper_title: Investments and Borrowing Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Council holds £20.3m in non-treasury investments comprising direct capital loans to service providers and limited companies
findings.detail: Beyond its £8.4m long-term and £0.1m short-term treasury investments, the Council has £20.3 million placed directly as capital loans to specific service providers and limited companies. These represent contingent credit exposures outside the standard PWLB debt structure; default by any of these entities would create unexpected losses or require council support.
findings.matters: Concentrated equity-like investments in service providers create contingent liabilities not reflected in PWLB borrowing figures. A lender needs to understand both the explicit debt (£94.1m PWLB) and these implicit credit exposures.
findings.figures: £20.3 million in non-treasury investments
findings.quote: The Council also has £20.3 million in non-treasury investments which is made up of capital loans to specific service providers and limited companies.

findings.paper_title: Investments and Borrowing Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Council realized £738k capital loss on UBS Multi-Asset Fund, depleting investment loss mitigation reserve from £1.15m to £412k
findings.detail: The Council closed its UBS Multi-Asset Fund on 16 September 2025 and realized a capital loss of £738k on an initial investment of £3.0m. The Investment Performance Equalisation reserve was drawn down from £1,150k to £412k to cover this loss. However, the remaining long-term investments held a carrying capital loss of £572k at 31 March 2026, meaning the depleted reserve covers only 72% of remaining unrealized losses.
findings.matters: Material investment losses erode financial resilience and available reserves. With the mitigation reserve now at £412k but remaining unrealized losses at £572k, the council has minimal protection against further portfolio deterioration.
findings.figures: £738k realized loss on £3.0m initial investment; mitigation reserve reduced from £1,150k to £412k; remaining carrying loss of £572k on other investments
findings.quote: With the closure of the UBS Multi-Asset Fund on 16 September the Council realised a capital loss of £738k on its initial investment of £3.0m. The use of the Investment Performance Equalisation reserve to mitigate will reduce the reserve to £412k.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Housing General Fund - Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Council proposing 54% increase in Disabled Facilities Grant spending through new annual bids of £228,200
findings.detail: The capital programme shows planned expansion of DFG spending from the current £420,000 to £648,200 in 2026-27. The new bids total £228,200 annually and are driven by the district's growing ageing population. The programme acknowledges that demand for adaptation work is difficult to predict but is known to be growing.
findings.matters: Shows the council's planned response to demographic change through increased social care investment, though the finance director should verify how the expansion beyond Better Care Fund's current funding level is resourced
findings.figures: £420,000 current programme; £228,200 new bids 2026-27; £648,200 total proposed 2026-27; £30,000 mandatory grant maximum per applicant
findings.quote: Central government funding is provided through the Better Care Fund (BCF) which covers the current level of expenditure

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Warm Homes Wave 3 brings £3.3m grant funding but execution risk on retrofit delivery timeline
findings.detail: Tandridge secured £3,263,885 in government grant (2025-2028) to retrofit 450 properties with energy efficiency measures. Phase 1 is underway retrofitting 130 homes plus 150 others; phases 2 and 3 (each 160 homes) remain unsubmitted and will be shaped by stock condition survey data. Slippage in delivery could affect grant compliance and require council funding of any gaps.
findings.matters: Externally funded capital reduces borrowing need, but if retrofit work doesn't meet grant timescales or conditions, the council may face unbudgeted fill-in costs or reputational risk with funders.
findings.figures: £3,263,885 grant over 3 years; 2026-27 estimated spend £2,355,000; 450 homes targeted
findings.quote: Tandridge were successful in securing £3,263,885 in grant funding over the next 3 years, to improve 450 properties within the stock.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA IT capital projects flagged as requiring business cases before they can proceed
findings.detail: The HRA IT capital budget (£46,300 in 2026-27) covers disaster recovery, system replacement cycles, and software upgrades. The document explicitly states these schemes lack the business case approval needed before progression can begin—a governance flag that capital has been allocated to schemes not yet formally evaluated.
findings.matters: Capital budgets typically assume business cases have been approved; flagging that IT schemes require business cases before proceeding means the council is committing budget to undefined investment decisions.
findings.quote: ** These schemes require a business case before the programme can be progressed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Council house building programme includes expected expenditure not yet formally approved
findings.detail: The council has budgeted £18.5m for council house building in 2026-27 (part of a £40.2m three-year total), but the document explicitly notes this includes expenditure awaiting Housing Committee approval. The phrasing 'as the expenditure will most likely be incurred' indicates capital spend is being forecast as committed before formal approval is secured.
findings.matters: A lender would require confidence that major capital commitments go through proper governance before spend is incurred; budgeting for unapproved expenditure as 'likely' raises questions about approval sequencing and budget control.
findings.quote: *Council House Building includes expected unapproved expenditure that will be brought to Housing Committee for approval as the expenditure will most likely be incurred.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026/27 Proposed Budget
findings.headline: Capital programme assumes 20% annual slippage (£3.7m) reflecting historical delivery challenges
findings.detail: £29.9m capital programme has been discounted by 20% to reflect programme slippage based on historical performance data. This represents £3.7m annual delivery shortfall factored into forecasts. Affects council's ability to deliver 40 new homes per year target.
findings.matters: Indicates persistent capital programme execution challenges. Only ~32 homes delivered annually despite 40-home target, reducing progress on housing supply and return on capital investment.
findings.figures: 20% slippage rate assumed, £3.7m annual slippage, £29.9m total capital programme, £18.5m Council House Building element
findings.quote: The programme has been discounted by 20% to reflect the programme slippage which is based on historical data this equates to £3.7m slippage.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026/27 Proposed Budget
findings.headline: £3.95m PWLB loan being refinanced at 3.96%, up from 3.0% original rate—96 basis point increase
findings.detail: £3.95m loan due for repayment 28 March 2027 with 3.0% fixed rate is being refinanced. Council has budgeted new PWLB rate (after discounts) at 3.96%, representing 96 basis point increase in borrowing cost.
findings.matters: Demonstrates rising interest rate pressures on debt refinancing. Annual interest cost increases by approximately £38k on this single loan, illustrating financial impact of higher PWLB rates on debt servicing.
findings.figures: £3.95m loan, 3.0% original rate to 3.96% new rate, 96 basis point increase
findings.quote: A £3.95m loan is scheduled to be repaid (on 28 th March 2027). This loan has a fixed interest rate of 3.0%. The new PWLB rate for this rolled over loan is budgeted to be (after discounts) 3.96%.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026/27 Proposed Budget
findings.headline: HRA debt increasing by £14.6m to £91.1m total, with interest costs assumed at 3.96%
findings.detail: HRA borrowing starting at £76.5m (£45.7m PWLB, £30.8m internal) will increase by £14.6m in 2026/27 to fund capital programme, reaching £91.1m total. Budget assumes PWLB rates at 3.96% after standard discounts.
findings.matters: Represents 19% debt growth in a single year. Material increase in leverage and debt service costs. Significant refinancing risk if rates rise further or if debt service capacity changes.
findings.figures: £76.5m current HRA debt, £91.1m projected, £14.6m additional borrowing 2026/27, 3.96% assumed PWLB rate
findings.quote: On the 1st April 2026 the HRA will have £76.5m of debt outstanding being loans with PWLB of £45.7m and internal borrowing from the General Fund of £30.8m. In the Budget 2026/27 the borrowing will increase by a further £14.6m. The total debt outstanding will be £91.1m.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026/27 Proposed Budget
findings.headline: Homes England capital grant funding access suspended due to C4 status, forcing increased borrowing
findings.detail: Council had Investment Partner status with Homes England and received £6.49m in grant funding since September 2023. All bidding for grants is now paused due to C4 regulatory status. Forces substitution with borrowing to fund capital programme.
findings.matters: Removes access to non-debt capital funding and forces higher-cost PWLB borrowing. Increases leverage and interest costs; demonstrates how regulatory failures have direct financial consequences.
findings.figures: £6.49m grant funding received to date now paused; £18.5m Council House Building programme requires funding
findings.quote: Currently there is a pause of Homes England bidding for grant due to the Council's C4 Status.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026/27 Proposed Budget
findings.headline: C4 regulatory rating due to unaddressed audit recommendations on health and safety compliance
findings.detail: Internal audit of Asset Management Health and Safety Compliance in 2024 identified high-priority issues. Failure to address these fully and timely contributed to the C4 regulatory rating. The council has increased compliance budgets to address consumer standards failures, particularly health, safety and asset management.
findings.matters: C4 status indicates significant governance and service delivery failures with implications for management capability. It is directly blocking access to capital funding and signals regulatory intervention risk.
findings.figures: C4 rating assigned; multiple consumer standards failures; audit recommendations outstanding
findings.quote: Failure to address the audit recommendations fully and in a timely manner has contributed to the regulatory judgement of C4.

findings.paper_title: Housing Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Internal audit found high-priority health and safety gaps in asset management requiring remedial spending
findings.detail: An internal audit of Asset Management Health and Safety Compliance "highlighted several high priorities in relation to the management of the Councils assets." As a result, the council has increased compliance budgets and procured contracts for electrical testing, asbestos removal, and water risk assessments, and will complete stock condition surveys and Energy Performance Certificates.
findings.matters: High-priority audit findings indicate pre-existing governance gaps in safety compliance. The need for emergency remedial spending on electrical, asbestos and water safety during transition period signals operational risk that was not previously captured.
findings.figures: Multiple urgent compliance contracts: electrical testing, asbestos removal, water risk assessments, stock condition survey, Energy Performance Certificates
findings.quote: An internal audit of Asset Management Health and Safety Compliance was undertaken earlier this year. The audit highlighted several high priorities in relation to the management of the Councils assets.

findings.paper_title: Housing Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Government homelessness grant falling by £60k while demand pressure is rising
findings.detail: Ongoing pressures include a £60k anticipated reduction in Government Grant for homelessness, occurring at the same time the council is facing £200k additional pressure for temporary accommodation. This is a misalignment between funding and demand.
findings.matters: Central government is cutting homelessness funding while demand pressures rise, forcing the council to absorb increased costs from its own resources during a period of financial stress.
findings.figures: Homelessness grant reduction: £60k
findings.quote: £60k anticipated reduction in Government Grant for homelessness.

findings.paper_title: Housing Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs rising unpredictably with £200k one-off pressure provision
findings.detail: Housing Committee faces £200k one-off pressure for potential increases in temporary accommodation demand. The paper explicitly warns: "Due to the unpredictable nature in estimating temporary accommodation costs this will be monitored very carefully by the service in 2026/27." This signals management concern about volatile, demand-driven costs.
findings.matters: Rising temporary accommodation costs and unpredictability indicate growing homelessness pressure in the district, a service cost that is difficult to control and signals wider social/economic stress.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation one-off pressure: £200k
findings.quote: Due to the unpredictable nature in estimating temporary accommodation costs this will be monitored very carefully by the service in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Housing Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: £2.4m one-off pressures, mostly Local Government Reorganisation costs, being funded from reserves
findings.detail: One-off pressures total £2.4m: £1.5m for LGR-related costs (including £0.9m interim costs and £0.6m TDC contribution to pre-vesting costs), £0.6m planning appeals, £0.1m Community Asset Transfer, £0.2m homelessness. All funded from usable reserves (£2.173m). The council states explicitly: "The sustainability for the Council to be in a position to continue year on year funding similar amounts of one-off LGR £1.5m costs year on year would not be possible to do so."
findings.matters: A lender should understand the scale and nature of transition costs and whether they can be absorbed. The £1.5m annual LGR cost being unsustainable signals the transition is financially straining.
findings.figures: Total one-off pressures: £2.4m; LGR costs: £1.5m (interim: £0.9m, pre-vesting: £0.6m); planning: £0.6m; homelessness: £0.2m; funded from reserves: £2.173m
findings.quote: The sustainability for the Council to be in a position to continue year on year funding similar amounts of one-off LGR £1.5m costs year on year would not be possible to do so.

findings.paper_title: Housing Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Budget draws on reserves to balance, with legal warnings that reserves are already low and at risk
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget uses £0.2m from reserves to reach balance. The council's legal section flags that the General Fund reserve (£3m) is already low, and notes: "Reliance on the Council's already low General Fund reserves to achieve balance represents a risk to financial resilience" and warns that further in-year pressures could exceed available reserves, requiring urgent mitigation.
findings.matters: A council drawing reserves to balance budget signals financial stress; legal warnings about reserve adequacy are red flags for a lender about the council's ability to handle unexpected cost pressures through transition.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve: £3m; 2026/27 draw: £0.2m; net pressures: £0.6m
findings.quote: Reliance on the Council's already low General Fund reserves to achieve balance represents a risk to financial resilience, reducing the Council's ability to respond to unforeseen pressures during the transition to the new unitary authority on 1 April 2027.

findings.paper_title: Housing Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Council is being abolished on 1 April 2027 and transferred to East Surrey Council
findings.detail: This is Tandridge's final budget-setting cycle. The council will cease to exist after 31 March 2027 and be subsumed into a new unitary authority. The budget must balance service continuity with the constraint of avoiding new long-term commitments, since decisions on future structures and contracts will rest with the successor authority.
findings.matters: A lender assessing lending to the council needs to understand continuity risk through the transition period and whether the council maintains financial stability until handover.
findings.figures: Abolition: 1 April 2027
findings.quote: As the Council will cease as an entity after 31st March 2027 the MTFS is only for one-year only (rather than the usual three to four years).

findings.paper_title: Capital Investment and Treasury Management Strategy - Tandridge Covering Report 26-27
findings.headline: HRA capital financing requirement grows to £120.6m, driven by capital investment in stock condition surveys and safety and legislation compliance
findings.detail: The HRA CFR is increasing from £106.7m to £120.6m over the three-year strategy period. The council attributes this growth specifically to a further year of capital spend brought into scope (2027/28) and to increased capital spending linked to recent stock condition surveys and compliance with safety and legislative changes. The strategy projects annual growth in HRA CFR over the planning period.
findings.matters: Growing HRA debt represents an increasing financial commitment for the council. Lenders need to understand both the drivers of this capital investment and the council's plan to service the additional borrowing.
findings.figures: HRA CFR grows to £120.6m over the period (from £106.7m in the previous strategy)
findings.quote: The HRA CFR grows to £120.6m over the period (from £106.7m in the previous strategy). The increase is largely linked to 2 things a further year of capital spend (i.e. 2027/28) brought into scope for the MTFS and increased capital spend due to the recent stock condition surveys and the HRA striving to ensure the stock is compliment with safety and legislation changes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Community Services - Capital Programme
findings.headline: Council has shifted vehicle strategy from leasing to purchasing, increasing future capital and potentially debt requirements.
findings.detail: The council has made a decision to "purchase vehicles rather than re new the lease once the lease has expired." This moves cost from the revenue/lease line to capital purchases, potentially increasing borrowing needs.
findings.matters: A strategic shift from leasing to purchasing increases capital requirements and may increase borrowing needs, changing the council's future cash flow and debt profile.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Also the Council has also taken the decision to purchase vehicles rather than re new the lease once the lease has expired.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Community Services - Capital Programme
findings.headline: Sports Pavilions capital budget is not being spent to plan due to emergency improvements diverting resources.
findings.detail: The council has set aside capital budget for Sports Pavilions but states "the programme of works to complete this has not been strictly adhered to, due to other emergency improvements taking priority." It is now developing a revised programme. This indicates either poor planning or unforeseen demands crowding out scheduled work.
findings.matters: Capital slippage can indicate either forecasting errors or that the council is responding to emergencies at the expense of planned work. A lender needs to know whether capital plans are achievable or whether real demand is different from the forecast.
findings.figures: Budget amount not disclosed
findings.quote: Although there has been a capital budget set aside for Sports Pavilions, the programme of works to complete this has not been strictly adhered to, due to other emergency improvements taking priority.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Community Services - Capital Programme
findings.headline: Years of deferred land drainage maintenance now creating risk of large-scale future expenditure.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges "lack of structural maintenance over a number of years" leaving ditches full of silt and detritus. It warns that without action, "sports pitch drainage systems as they will become blocked and large scale expenditure will be incurred to rectify blockages." This is a classic deferred maintenance trap where lack of small ongoing costs creates risk of much larger bills.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance is a leading indicator of financial stress and increases future capital demands. A lender would want to know whether this is being caught in time or whether other pressures are preventing routine upkeep.
findings.figures: None provided; scope implied as multi-year backlog across sports facilities
findings.quote: Due to the lack of structural maintenance over a number of years the ditches are full of silt and detritus. The surrounding vegetation is also encroaching over the ditch / land drainage area.

findings.paper_title: Community Services Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Failure of the Biffa waste contract to deliver statutory waste and recycling collections is identified as a key operational risk.
findings.detail: Biffa is the contractor for statutory waste and recycling collections across the district. 'Failure of Biffa to deliver the statutory waste and recycling collections' is listed in the key risks section, with no mitigation described. Statutory waste collection is a duty the council cannot suspend.
findings.matters: Loss of waste collection would be a service failure and a statutory breach. In a final-year council without time to recover, this would be a serious operational problem.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Failure of Biffa to deliver the statutory waste and recycling collections.

findings.paper_title: Community Services Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Service continuity for community and voluntary grants is at risk, with potential reduction in services to vulnerable residents.
findings.detail: The council identifies continuity of community and voluntary grants as a key risk. The paper states this may lead to a reduction in services to vulnerable residents. While the council is working to find multi-year funding agreements and alternative funding, this is identified as an ongoing risk that mitigation is still being worked through.
findings.matters: A council that cannot guarantee service continuity to vulnerable residents in its final year signals potential service collapse during transition. Alternative funding and joint ventures with other authorities are aspirational, not confirmed.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Continuity with Community and Voluntary grants may lead to a reduction in services to vulnerable residents. To mitigate the impact on these organisations work will continue to look at multi-year funding agreements and to seek alternative funding opportunities and joint ventures with other authorities.

findings.paper_title: Community Services Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: The Tandridge Lottery has seen significantly reduced ticket sales, cutting income to the Community Fund supporting vulnerable residents.
findings.detail: The council identifies as a key risk that the Tandridge Lottery is experiencing reduced ticket sales due to cost of living pressures. The reduction in sales directly impacts funding available through the Tandridge Community Fund, which supports vulnerable residents. This is a discretionary income stream that is now declining.
findings.matters: This shows income volatility from a service that depends on discretionary resident spending. As a final-year council, the ability to rebuild this income stream does not exist. Vulnerable residents may see services reduced or transferred with less planning.
findings.figures: Lottery ticket sales declining; impact not quantified
findings.quote: With continuing cost of living expenses, the Tandridge Lottery has seen reduced ticket sales. The reduction in sales has a direct impact on the overall community and voluntary organisations through the Tandridge Community Fund.

findings.paper_title: Community Services Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: The council is not planning to deliver its normal £1 million annual savings requirement due to uncertainty about what the successor authority will want.
findings.detail: Historically the council has delivered around £1 million of permanent savings annually to match spending pressures. For 2026/27, only £0.4m of savings are being sought. The council's explicit reasoning is that most savings require investment in technology, staffing restructures, or new contracts—decisions that should rest with the successor authority, not a council in its final year. This leaves an ongoing structural gap in the budget that is accepted as unavoidable.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural gap that cannot be closed without service reductions or other changes that the council says are not its decision to make. A lender needs to understand that £0.6m of recurring pressures are being met by reserve drawdown and funding volatility reserves, not by sustainable savings.
findings.figures: £1 million usual annual savings requirement; £0.4 million planned for 2026/27; £0.6m net recurring pressures
findings.quote: For this reason, the Council is not planning to deliver the full £1 million of savings for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Community Services Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: The council's legal officer has flagged that already low General Fund reserves are being used to achieve budget balance, creating a risk to financial resilience.
findings.detail: The Monitoring Officer has explicitly warned that reliance on low reserves to balance the budget reduces the council's ability to respond to unforeseen pressures during transition. More critically, there remains a stated risk that further pressures emerging during the year could exceed available reserves, which would require urgent in-year mitigation. This warning appears in the formal legal implications section of the budget paper.
findings.matters: This is a direct statement from the Monitoring Officer that the council may not have sufficient reserves to cope with in-year pressures. A council that cannot absorb unexpected costs in its final year could face service disruption or be forced into emergency action.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve stable at £3 million (from paragraph 2.4); described as 'already low'
findings.quote: Reliance on the Council's already low General Fund reserves to achieve balance represents a risk to financial resilience, reducing the Council's ability to respond to unforeseen pressures during the transition to the new unitary authority on 1 April 2027. There remains a risk that further pressures emerging during the year could exceed available reserves, requiring urgent in-year mitigation.

findings.paper_title: Community Services Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: The council is drawing down £2.173m from usable reserves to fund one-off reorganisation pressures, on top of regular budget pressures.
findings.detail: One-off pressures total £2.4m, predominantly from local government reorganisation costs (£1.5m, including £0.7m interim costs and £0.6m contribution to pre-vesting day costs). Other one-off pressures of £0.9m include planning appeals, election costs, and homelessness costs. These are being funded from usable reserves (£2.173m) plus £0.2m from creditors holding previous homelessness grant. This significantly depletes the reserve base.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund current spending rather than one-off items represents a draw on financial resilience. When a council is in its final year of existence, the ability to recover that depleted reserve through future surpluses does not exist.
findings.figures: £2.4m one-off pressures; £2.173m from usable reserves; £1.5m LGR costs; £0.9m other one-off costs
findings.quote: In addition to the budget pressures as above there are also this year one-off pressures of £2.4m. Most of the one-off pressures relate to additional cost of establishing the new East Surrey Unitary.

findings.paper_title: Community Services Committee - 2026/27 Proposed General Fund Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: The council will cease to exist on 1 April 2027 as a separate entity, fundamentally changing the nature of this budget.
findings.detail: Tandridge District Council is being abolished as part of Surrey local government reorganisation. The council's functions will be transferred to a new East Surrey Unitary on 1 April 2027. This is the final year the council will set its own budget; the medium-term financial strategy covers only one year instead of the usual three or four. All future capital investment decisions from 2027/28 onwards will rest with the new unitary authorities.
findings.matters: A lending decision to a council that ceases to exist in nine months is entirely different from lending to a going concern. All assets, liabilities and contracts transfer; the council cannot enter new long-term commitments.
findings.figures: Abolished 1 April 2027; MTFS covers 2026/27 only
findings.quote: As the Council will cease as an entity after 31st March 2027 the MTFS is for one-year only (rather than the usual three to four years). The focus of the year to 31st March 2027 is on ensuring a stable, legally compliant, and fully documented final year budget, alongside a comprehensive financial handover to the new authority.

findings.paper_title: Tandridge DC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 for Audit Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: 2024/25 accounts published on time for first time in three years; prior years 2022/23 and 2023/24 remain unaudited
findings.detail: The council published its 2024/25 accounts on 30 June 2025, meeting the statutory deadline for the first time in three years and removing a significant weakness from the audit assessment. However, the auditor notes that the 2022/23 and 2023/24 financial statements remain unaudited due to the wider audit backlog.
findings.matters: While timely publication of current accounts is positive, the fact that two prior years remain unaudited creates uncertainty about historical financial position and creates an audit validation gap.
findings.figures: 3-year improvement in accounts timeliness
findings.quote: The Council published a comprehensive set of 2024/25 accounts before the statutory deadline of 30 June for the first time in three years, which removes the significant weakness from the Council's arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Tandridge DC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 for Audit Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £4.35m in 2024/25; HRA housing schemes affected by contractor failures
findings.detail: The council reported net forecast slippage of £4.35m in the capital programme (£1.31m General Fund, £3.04m HRA housing schemes). The council has experienced difficulties with housing contractors going into administration, leading to delays and cost pressures in HRA scheme delivery.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage indicates project delivery risk and may signal challenges in the council's ability to execute its capital strategy; contractor failures on housing schemes carry both cost and service quality implications.
findings.figures: £4.35m total slippage; £1.31m General Fund; £3.04m HRA
findings.quote: Capital Programme Outturn was a Net Forecast Slippage of £4.35m, of which £1.31m is due to General Fund capital projects and £3.04m due to slippage on HRA housing schemes.

findings.paper_title: Tandridge DC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 for Audit Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Planning service significantly underperforming; Local Plan deemed unsound by Planning Inspectorate
findings.detail: Major planning applications are being approved at only 55% (significantly below performance benchmarks), and the Planning Inspectorate concluded in February 2024 that the council's Local Plan is not sound and should not be adopted. The council is developing a Planning Improvement Plan to integrate development management and strategic planning.
findings.matters: Planning underperformance delays income from S106/CIL contributions and reduces the council's ability to fund infrastructure or generate capital receipts; an unsound Local Plan hampers development and housing delivery.
findings.figures: 55% major planning application approval rate
findings.quote: The Planning Inspectorate concluding in February 2024 that it is not sound and should not be adopted.

findings.paper_title: Tandridge DC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 for Audit Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is complicating savings delivery; investments are limited to one-year payback
findings.detail: The planned reorganisation of Surrey's 11 districts and county council into two unitary councils from 1 April 2027 is constraining the council's ability to identify and deliver savings. The council has decided that significant investment in 2026/27 will only take place where there is assurance the solution will remain in place for the successor authority, making longer-term technology and service investments unviable.
findings.matters: LGR removes the council's ability to invest in operational efficiencies or transformational savings; this structural constraint makes the £4m gap harder to close and increases implementation risk.
findings.figures: Successor authority date: 1 April 2027
findings.quote: LGR has complicated efforts to identify savings as any investments or restructures would only guarantee a one-year payback period and delivery will be difficult, as they often require investment in technology, staffing changes, or external services.

findings.paper_title: Tandridge DC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 for Audit Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: General Fund reserve of £2.97m will be exhausted by end of 2027/28 if savings targets are not met
findings.detail: The council holds a General Fund reserve of only £2.97m, which auditors warn will be exhausted by the end of 2027/28 if sufficient savings are not delivered each year. This is a low reserve position for a district council and creates vulnerability to unforeseen pressures or shortfalls in delivery of planned savings.
findings.matters: Rapidly depleting reserves signal that the council has very limited buffer for service pressures or savings shortfalls; lenders track reserve depletion as a leading indicator of distress.
findings.figures: £2.97m General Fund reserve as at 31 March 2025; £9.48m earmarked reserves
findings.quote: The Council's General Fund reserve is low at only £2.966m and will be exhausted by the end of 2027/28 if sufficient savings are not made each year to balance the budgets for the next few years.

findings.paper_title: Tandridge DC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 for Audit Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: £4m funding gap over MTFS with insufficient recurrent savings identified
findings.detail: The council faces a £4m financial challenge over its Medium-Term Financial Strategy to 2028/29, requiring recurrent annual savings of around £1m per annum. However, the council has only identified £0.75m savings for 2025/26 and £0.44m for 2026/27, falling significantly short of the £1m target. In 2024/25 the council delivered only £0.49m against target (82% delivery).
findings.matters: A persistent savings shortfall is a leading indicator of structural budget stress; lenders and finance directors need to understand whether the council can close a £4m gap or will be forced into more drastic action.
findings.figures: £4m MTFS gap; £1m per annum target; £0.75m 2025/26 plan; £0.44m 2026/27 plan; £0.49m 2024/25 delivery
findings.quote: The Council faces a significant financial challenge, with a £4m gap over its Medium-Term Financial Strategy to 2028/29. The Council needs to identify more savings closer to its savings target of £1m a year

findings.paper_title: Tandridge DC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 for Audit Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Housing service rated C4 (very serious failings) by Regulator of Social Housing
findings.detail: The council's housing service has been graded as C4 by the Regulator of Social Housing, indicating very serious failings and significant improvement needed. The council self-referred following an internal review that identified electrical safety testing had not been properly carried out. Weaknesses identified include Transparency and Accountability Standard, Tenancy Standard, and aspects of Safety and Quality Standards. The council is working on a remedial action plan that will create budget pressures for the Housing Revenue Account.
findings.matters: A C4 regulatory rating represents a material failure in social housing standards and signals both immediate cost exposure (remedial works) and reputational risk that affects the council's creditworthiness and landlord function.
findings.figures: 2,600 council homes affected; remedial action plan due 28 February 2026
findings.quote: The "C4" rating indicated "very serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvement is needed."

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Quarter 2 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Warm Home 3 decarbonisation scheme significantly underperforming with £400k underspend due to uptake and resource issues
findings.detail: The scheme is achieving substantially less uptake than budgeted, with £400k underspend resulting from promotion, access, and resource constraints. The council is aiming to recruit a tenant liaison officer to improve take-up rates.
findings.matters: A capital scheme underperforming by £400k indicates delivery and engagement challenges, raising questions about the council's ability to execute energy efficiency and housing improvement targets.
findings.figures: £400k underspend; scheme seeking to recruit tenant liaison officer
findings.quote: (£400k) underspend of Warm Home 3 scheme  – There has been less take up of the scheme due to  promotion/ access issues and resources – the service is aiming to recruit a tenant liaison officer to gain access and carry out more surveys.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Quarter 2 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator has required new compliance-focused staff positions
findings.detail: The council has been required to create new permanent roles specifically to address regulator-identified gaps. These positions focus on compliance and operational issues including Health and Safety, Damp and Mould, ASB Support, Temporary Housing, and Leaseholder Services.
findings.matters: Regulatory requirements to add compliance staff indicate governance or operational weaknesses that represent a credit risk for lenders, suggesting the council may need ongoing regulatory oversight.
findings.figures: £162k salary budget allocated for these positions in 2025/26
findings.quote: These positions include Health and safety specialist and new posts including an additional ASB Support Officer and Temporary Housing Officer, a Leaseholder and Service Charge Manager and a Damp and Mould Property Support Officer.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Quarter 2 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspent by £310k at Q2, primarily driven by regulatory compliance staffing costs
findings.detail: HRA is £310k over budget at month 6. £162k of salary overspend is due to interim staff and new permanent positions required by the Social Housing Regulator. Additional costs include £78k in service costs and £69k in repairs and maintenance.
findings.matters: A £310k Q2 overspend suggests a likely significant year-end overspend that will require either reserve drawdown or budget correction, affecting the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £310k total overspend; £162k salary; £78k service costs; £69k repairs
findings.quote:
Housing Revenue Account overspend £310k  mainly due to : -
£162k (net overspend) Salaries  - mainly due to the use of interims to cover vacancies and additional permanent roles to help deliver improvements needed as identified by the Social Housing Regulator.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 2 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Emerging risks in homelessness and housing benefit costs flagged as potential full-year variances
findings.detail: The council reports that risks around homelessness costs and housing benefit expenses are being monitored and managed, but explicitly notes these 'may present as a variance later in the financial year'. These are not yet quantified as overspends but the council is flagging them as emerging pressures.
findings.matters: Homelessness and benefit pressures are volatile demand-led costs that can escalate rapidly; flagging these early indicates the council expects additional spending that is not yet reflected in the forecast.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Risks to the General Fund budget around Homelessness and the cost of Housing Benefit are being monitored, managed and may present as a variance later in the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 2 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Additional £107k drawn from HRA reserves to fund Social Housing Regulator compliance requirements
findings.detail: Following the Social Housing Regulator's review, the council is requesting a further £107k transfer from HRA reserves to the Housing Improvement Plan, in addition to the £420k already allocated earlier in the year. This brings total reserve drawdowns to £527k of the original £6,207k HRA operating surplus.
findings.matters: Drawing reserves to meet regulatory compliance requirements indicates the operating budget is insufficient and the council must rely on accumulated reserves, reducing its financial cushion for unforeseen pressures.
findings.figures: £107k additional transfer; £420k previously transferred; £6,207k original HRA operating surplus
findings.quote: It is requested that a further £107k is transferred from the HRA reserves to the Housing Improvement Plan (HIP) budget.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 2 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecasting £310k full-year overspend despite £5.8m operating surplus
findings.detail: At Month 6, the HRA which was budgeted to have a net operating surplus of £5,787k is now forecasting a full-year revenue budget variance of £310k overspend. This represents a significant deterioration from the budgeted surplus and indicates the housing service is consuming more resources than planned.
findings.matters: For lenders, an HRA overspend signals that the council's housing revenue is under pressure and resources are being consumed faster than anticipated, reducing financial flexibility and available reserves for investment or emergencies.
findings.figures: £310k full-year overspend forecast; against £5,787k budgeted operating surplus
findings.quote: At Month 6 (September), a full year revenue budget variance of £310k overspend is forecast for the Housing Revenue Account.

findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether this was planned seasonal cash flow movement or indicated unexpected liquidity stress.

The document provides no explanation of whether this was a strategic redemption or investment loss.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether this represents a strategic decision or investment underperformance that affected the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Original investment £3,000,000; prior year return £57,370; current net asset value £0

findings.detail: Non-treasury investments total £20.32m and are entirely held in Gryllus: £11.66m Castlefield loan at 6.10%, £2.39m Maidstone loan at 5.81%, £1.01m Station Road loan at 5.43%, and £5.25m share capital (forecast to pay no dividend). findings.detail: Funding Circle holding was withdrawn almost completely in 2024/25, going from £160,449 opening value to £1,871 closing value via a £162,320 withdrawal. This investment had accumulated £111,152 in bad debts in 2018/19 alone.
findings.matters: Exit from high-risk peer-to-peer lending after experiencing material bad debts shows risk reduction or poor performance; signals council's treasury moving toward lower-risk strategy.

findings.detail: The UBS Multi Asset Fund holding has been liquidated completely; it shows as £0 carrying value for 2024/25 and 2025/26, having been held at £3,000,000 every year from 2018/19. The fund had shown cumulative capital losses, including a £792,158 loss in 2023/24.
findings.matters: Withdrawal from a major (one-third of the original portfolio) investment vehicle signals either performance concerns, or that the council needed the liquidity; material change to investment holdings worth noting.
findings.figures: £3,000,000 position reduced to £0; 2023/24 capital loss (£792,158)

findings.paper_title: Item 4_Summary investment and borrowing position at 30 September 2025 Final
findings.headline: IFRS 9 statutory override expires April 2029, exposing £8.6 million long-term investment fund to fair value volatility
findings.detail: Long-term investments of £8.6 million are currently protected from fair value movements by the IFRS 9 override. An Investment Performance Equalisation reserve of £412k covers current carrying losses of £405k. Protection ends 1 April 2029, after which fair value movements will impact reserves and budget.
findings.matters: Fair value exposure on £8.6 million of investments from 2029 onwards will create potential balance sheet volatility and reserve calls affecting borrowing headroom
findings.figures: £8.6 million in long-term investments; reserve balance £412k; current carrying loss £405k; override expires 1 April 2029
findings.quote: With the override in place, Councils remove the impact of fair value movements on these funds from their budgets and record them in an unusable reserve on the Balance Sheet. This continues to apply to the long-term investments held by the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 4_Summary investment and borrowing position at 30 September 2025 Final

findings.detail: Beyond £12.9 million in treasury investments, the council has £20.3 million deployed as capital loans to specific service providers and limited companies. This represents significant exposure to non-standardised instruments with operational and counterparty concentration risk.
findings.matters: Non-treasury investments in service providers and companies carry different risk profiles than tradeable securities; lenders need visibility on these exposures and their performance
findings.figures: £20.3 million in capital loans to specific service providers and limited companies
findings.quote: The Council also has £20.3 million in non-treasury investments which is made up of capital loans to specific service providers and limited companies.

findings.matters: Repeated reliance on short-term borrowing indicates predictable but material cash flow timing mismatches that lenders assess as ongoing liquidity risk

findings.quote: The Council has needed to borrow on a short-term basis (ranging from one to 15 days) on four occasions in the first half of the year. This has been to overcome temporary cash shortages at the end of April, May, June and July

It is holding a £75k unallocated inflation allowance corporately specifically to help mitigate inflationary risks on the waste contract and grounds maintenance contract.
findings.matters: Waste services are typically one of the largest operational costs for a district council. Unresolved inflation exposure of this scale, requiring contingency reserves to be held back, indicates genuine uncertainty about cost control in a major service area.

findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council faces structural pressures that might affect debt servicing capability. The council's own assessment that additional funding is needed despite currently being close to balanced at Q2 indicates genuine medium-term stress.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme rephased down by £6.224m from £30.37m available budget to £24.15m, a 21% reduction
findings.detail: Available HRA capital budget of £30.370m (including £3.804m carry-forwards) is being rephased to £24.146m for 2025/26 following officers' review of likely timing and requirements. The resulting £6.224m underspend on available budget suggests either delayed delivery or changed priorities in housing investment.
findings.matters: Large reduction in planned housing capital spending could indicate scheme slippage, delivery challenges, or reprioritisation that affects the council's ability to deliver housing investment and signals to lenders about capital project execution.
findings.figures: Available budget £30,370k; rephased to £24,146k; £6,224k underspend; carry-forwards £3,804k
findings.quote: Whilst £30,370k is the available budget, officers considered the likely timing of capital expenditure and the amount required for 2025/26 in September 2025. Following this rephasing work for 2025/26, HRA Capital Programme Budget will be adjusted to a value of £24,146k. The current forecast is for a £6,224k underspend

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee
findings.headline: £425k new revenue expenditure approved for Housing Improvement Plan following Social Housing Regulator review
findings.detail: Following a pending review by the Social Housing Regulator, the committee is approving a £425k new revenue budget for a Housing Improvement Plan. Funding comes from £420k virement from the HRA budgeted surplus and £5k from Services Costs virement. This represents significant new spending driven by external regulatory scrutiny of housing services.
findings.matters: The improvement plan is a material new commitment (56% of the £750k General Fund housing budget) triggered by regulator review, indicating the council had issues requiring remedial action identified by external oversight.
findings.figures: £425k new spend; £420k from HRA surplus virement; £5k from Services Costs virement; HGF revenue budget £750k
findings.quote: Since the setting of the budget and pending a review by the Social Housing Regulator the service has put forward a Housing Improvement Plan as reported elsewhere on the agenda. It is proposed to set up a £425k revenue budget to facilitate the Housing Improvement Plan. £420k will be met by of virement from the HRA budgeted surplus

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 3 Q1 2025-26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee F.pptx
findings.headline: Homelessness spend is flagged as highly sensitive to temporary accommodation demand with potential for rapid budget impact
findings.detail: The report explicitly warns that 'Homelessness is very sensitive to changes in temporary accommodation costs' and 'a small increase in numbers can have a significant impact on the budget', despite current spend being 'in line with expectations'.
findings.matters: Homelessness volatility is a known source of budget pressure for councils. Even councils with reserves to mitigate the Housing Benefit impact face unbudgeted costs if TA numbers spike.
findings.figures: None disclosed; current spend in line but flagged as volatile
findings.quote: Risks are being managed within the budget, particularly in respect of Homelessness which is very sensitive to changes in temporary accommodation costs. Spend to-date is in line with expectations, but a small increase in numbers can have a significant impact on the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 3 Q1 2025-26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee F.pptx
findings.headline: Council is provisioning for compensation as it implements Housing Ombudsman code
findings.detail: The HRA shows £5.2k 'expected compensation as the authority works towards implementing the Housing Ombudsman code', suggesting prior non-compliance with ombudsman standards and ongoing remediation.
findings.matters: Ombudsman compensation signals service failure and governance gaps in housing management. It indicates the council was not compliant with consumer standards and is now paying to fix it.
findings.figures: £5.2k expected compensation
findings.quote: £5.2k in expected compensation as the authority works towards implementing the Housing Ombudsman code

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 3 Q1 2025-26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee F.pptx
findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator compliance review is due in August 2025 and costs are expected to increase beyond the current £25k provision
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £25k additional compliance works but explicitly states costs 'could increase further subject to the final report due in August'. This creates unquantified downside risk. Capital compliance spend is also elevated at £1,238k for fire safety, damp and mould works.
findings.matters: Regulatory uncertainty around Social Housing Regulator findings could impose unbudgeted costs. Compliance failures can trigger intervention or restrictions on housing operations.
findings.figures: £25k provision with further increases expected; £1,238k capital compliance spend
findings.quote: £25k additional Compliance works forecasted pending a review of the outcomes by the Social Housing Regulator – these costs could increase further subject to the final report due in August

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 3 Q1 2025-26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee F.pptx
findings.headline: Four major housing schemes totalling £8.3m are slipped: Featherstone, Pelham House, Warren Lane, and Sea Cadets
findings.detail: Capital scheme delivery is stalling across multiple projects. The slippage represents net (£9,629k) against these four named schemes, though partially offset by new schemes including Stychens Lane (£1,315k).
findings.matters: Large capital programme slippages indicate delivery risk and potential pressure on planned borrowing or government grant claims. They also delay housing supply outcomes the council has committed to.
findings.figures: (£9,629k) slippage on four named schemes
findings.quote: (£9,629k) of the slippage relates to the schemes Featherstone , Pelham House, Warren Lane and Sea Cadets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Month 3 Q1 2025-26 Budget Monitoring - Housing Committee F.pptx
findings.headline: Bronze Oak contractor has entered administration on a housing construction project, creating £765k cost overrun with latent defects outstanding
findings.detail: The document reports that a major contractor serving the council went into administration, leading to unexpected project costs and defects remediation. A performance bond of up to £772k is available to offset costs once the defect period ends in August 2026, but the council will need to manage the contractor failure and subsequent claims.
findings.matters: Contractor insolvency on capital schemes creates delivery delays, cost uncertainty, and administrative burden. It signals potential construction sector stress affecting councils' housing delivery.
findings.figures: £765k net overspend, £772k performance bond
findings.quote: £765k net overspend is mainly due to the Bronze oak contractor going into administration and the project costing more than anticipated and latent defects works at the Court scheme.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Capital budget for waste and garden waste bins reduced by £108k based on demand trends and storage constraints
findings.detail: Post-rollout demand for additional wheeled and recycling bins is lower than forecast. Council also cannot procure further bins due to storage capacity limitations, making a £108k capital reductions necessary for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Capital budget reduction indicates waste infrastructure rollout is largely complete and demand is stabilizing; affects future capital planning assumptions
findings.figures: £15k Garden Waste Bins + £93k Refuse/Recycling/Food Waste Bins reduction; total capital forecast £2,349k against £2,457k available
findings.quote: Demand trends since the roll out of wheeled bins and other recycling bins indicate not all of this budget is required for 2025-26 therefore the projection has been reduced accordingly. In addition, due to storage capacity issues it would be difficult to procure more bins for future use.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Animal Welfare Licensing income down £7k because better-performing businesses now qualify for longer licence periods
findings.detail: The licensing income budget was based on expected transaction frequency, but compliant businesses now receive longer licence terms, reducing the number of annual licensing transactions and therefore fee revenue.
findings.matters: Structural shift in licensing patterns; the revenue assumption was based on historical turnovers that no longer apply, indicating the budget needs recalibrating
findings.figures: £7k reduction in Animal Welfare Licensing income
findings.quote: £7k reduction in income from Animal Welfare Licensing which is based on standards so higher performing businesses qualify for a longer licence periods therefore varying the expected income levels achieved.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Unforeseen legal costs of £4k incurred in licensing notice appeals
findings.detail: Environmental Services recorded unexpected expenditure defending licensing enforcement decisions through appeal.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted litigation indicates regulatory or enforcement challenges; suggests either operational issues in licensing function or resistance to council decisions
findings.figures: £4k unforeseen legal costs
findings.quote: £4k from unforeseen legal costs of appealing licensing notices

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Streets & Public Conveniences overspending £30k as budgeted vacancy factor cannot be achieved
findings.detail: The service was budgeted with a staffing vacancy factor but is currently at full establishment, unable to reduce headcount as planned. This accounts for the majority of the £40k revenue overspend.
findings.matters: Indicates the council cannot operate this service at the staffing levels it forecast; either budgeted reductions are not feasible or the service requires full establishment, permanently raising costs
findings.figures: £30k overspend; budget £3,955k, forecast £3,995k
findings.quote: £30k Streets & Public Conveniences mainly down to the vacancy factor not being met due to a full establishment in this service.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Garden Waste income carries multiple identified risks despite high current membership, including potential changes to collection methods.
findings.detail: The paper flags ongoing risk to the Garden Waste income budget despite high membership. An additional uncertainty is introduced by a proposed change to collection methods, which could affect income levels. Some mitigation is possible from a waiting list.
findings.matters: Garden Waste is discretionary service income; operational changes to collection could drive membership loss and materially underperform this income line.
findings.figures: No specific amount quantified; identified as risk area despite high membership
findings.quote: A potential proposed change in Garden waste income collection methods may also affect income levels.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Animal Welfare Licensing income is down £7k because the council's own higher licensing standards mean better-performing businesses qualify for longer licence periods.
findings.detail: The licensing scheme allows higher-performing businesses to qualify for longer licence periods, reducing renewal frequency. This creates an unbudgeted £7k income loss, a structural pressure where the council's licensing success undermines its own revenue assumptions.
findings.matters: Revenue can be vulnerable to service-level policy decisions; this shows how the council's own standards can work against its budget projections.
findings.figures: £7k reduction in Animal Welfare Licensing income
findings.quote: £7k reduction in income from Animal Welfare Licensing which is based on standards so higher performing businesses qualify for a longer licence period therefore varying the expected income levels achieved

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Waste contract inflation is unquantified and could swing the budget forecast from surplus to deficit when rates are confirmed later in the year.
findings.detail: The paper identifies waste contract inflation as a material risk factor. Inflation rates are not yet confirmed, meaning the current forecast position holds this uncertainty and could deteriorate materially in either direction once actual inflation is known.
findings.matters: Waste services are a large operational budget; unquantified inflation on a major contract is a material cost exposure that could reverse the modest overspend into something larger.
findings.figures: Amount not specified; waste inflation rates to be confirmed later in year
findings.quote: Waste contract inflation - until inflation rates are confirmed later in the year, this could lead to a surplus or deficit against the budget.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 1 2025/26 Budget Monitoring - Community Services Committee
findings.headline: Streets and Public Conveniences overspending by £29k because the council cannot achieve its budgeted vacancy factor with a full establishment in post.
findings.detail: The paper forecasts a £29k overspend in Streets and Public Conveniences, explicitly attributing this to the vacancy factor not being met. The council's budget assumed staffing savings through vacancies, but the service has filled all posts and is now spending the full salary bill.
findings.matters: This is a structural budget management issue: the council cannot deliver planned savings through vacancies in this service, indicating either budget assumptions were unrealistic or staffing demands exceed budgeted levels.
findings.figures: £29k overspend in Streets and Public Conveniences
findings.quote: £29k mainly down to vacancy factor not being met due to a full establishment in post

news_drafts.headline: Grounds maintenance contract not mobilised fully and changes to scope manual and incomplete
news_drafts.lead: Incomplete contract mobilisation and unclear impact of scope changes on budget create cost control risk; manual, incomplete change management suggests budgetary slippage.

news_drafts.lead: A C4 housing regulator rating signals severe operational and governance failures in a major council service; this indicates both reputational and delivery risk, and may affect the council's standing with government.

news_drafts.headline: Business continuity plans missing for half of essential services, with no testing of those in place
news_drafts.lead: A council unable to execute business continuity for half its essential services poses operational and service delivery risk; lenders need confidence in operational resilience.
